text: Every activity in a pipeline offers four genuinely distinct outgoing paths, not just one: Upon Success, Upon Failure, Upon Completion, and Upon Skip. One real constraint worth remembering — Upon Completion can't coexist with Upon Success or Upon Failure on the same activity. You choose the success-failure split, or the single completion path.

The single most useful pattern in this lesson: a Copy job dies partway through, leaving a partial file behind. You want to clean that up without halting the rest of the pipeline. Connect the first activity's Upon Failure path to an error handler, then feed the next real activity from both the error handler's Upon Success path and the first activity's own Upon Skip path.

That Upon Skip connection is genuinely the trick that makes it work. If the first activity succeeds, the error handler gets skipped — and that skip itself satisfies the Upon Skip condition feeding the next activity, so the pipeline proceeds cleanly either way.

For a straightforward sequential chain, Copy, then Copy, then Copy, you often just want one shared handler at the end. Connect both the Upon Failure and Upon Skip paths of the very last activity in the chain into one generic error handler — it fires if anything upstream failed, and silently does nothing at all if everything succeeded.

Here's the detail that genuinely trips people up: defining an Upon Failure path doesn't automatically make the overall pipeline show Failed. Data Factory only evaluates leaf activities. Try-Catch, with just an Upon Failure path, still shows Success. Do-If-Else, with both Upon Failure and Upon Success defined, shows real Failure. Choose deliberately, based on whether you actually want a downstream alert to fire.

Four paths, two patterns, and one rule about how pipeline status actually gets decided. Next: Logging to Log Analytics — sending pipeline diagnostics somewhere you can actually query them, well beyond what the Monitor hub alone shows you.
